q: A team ships prompt changes after checking ten examples by eye. What is the most serious risk?
options: The examples are too short to read
Regressions on unseen cases go undetected because there is no baseline or coverage
The model will overfit to the ten examples through training
why: Without stored cases and baseline scores, a fix for one case can silently break others. Overfitting by training is not happening since the model is not trained on them.

q: Which assertion is appropriate for testing a free-text summariser?
options: Output contains all required action items and is under a length limit, over a pass-rate threshold
Output string equals a stored reference summary
Output has the same token count as before
Output is identical across five runs
why: Property checks tolerate varied wording; equality and identical-run checks produce false failures for valid output.

q: Why might a leaderboard-topping model underperform in your application?
options: Your prompts, retrieval, format and data differ from the benchmark tasks
why: Benchmarks measure generic tasks under their own prompt setups; your pipeline differs. Manipulation can happen but is not the general reason.

q: Production users report failures your eval set never covered. What is the best next step?
options: Categorise the failures and add representative cases and criteria to the eval dataset
why: Feeding real failures back closes the loop; changing thresholds or temperature does not add coverage.

q: Which evaluation signal is cheapest and most deterministic for verifying that output is valid JSON with required fields?
why: A validator is deterministic and free; judges and humans add cost and noise for a rule-checkable property.

q: An LLM judge was never compared to human labels. What is the main risk?
options: It will always give top scores
Its biases and misalignment with human preference go unnoticed, so scores may not mean what you think
why: Calibration against human labels shows whether the judge agrees with your standard; without it the metric is untrusted.

q: You monitor live chatbot traffic with no ground-truth answers. Which approach fits?
options: Wait for labels before measuring anything
Reference-free criteria such as faithfulness to context and safety
Compare to the golden dataset only
why: Live traffic has no labels, so reference-free scoring against criteria or context is the practical option.

q: A golden dataset of 1,500 cases scores 98%, yet users hit many failures. Most likely cause?
options: The set is dominated by near-duplicates and misses real edge cases
why: Low diversity inflates scores. Coverage and representativeness matter more than count.

q: Code generation outputs should most reliably be evaluated by:
options: Executing unit tests against the generated code
Asking the model if it is correct
why: Executable tests verify behaviour directly; self-assessment and style scores do not.

q: Your reference-based metric rates a correct paraphrased answer as wrong. Best fix?
options: Use semantic equivalence or a judge, or allow multiple references
why: String overlap penalises valid paraphrase; semantic equivalence handles it.

q: Which risk is a purely offline suite least able to detect?
options: A prompt change that breaks JSON formatting
A hosted model silently updated by the provider after release
A regression on a stored edge case
A lower retrieval recall on the golden set
why: Provider drift occurs live without code change; the other options are visible in a fixed offline set.

q: Why is p95 latency preferred over mean latency for monitoring?
options: It is more accurate for quality
It reveals tail slowness that averages hide
why: A few very slow requests barely move the mean but hurt real users; percentiles expose them.

q: Your dashboards show low latency and 0% errors, yet users complain about wrong answers. What is missing?
options: Quality metrics like faithfulness and correctness on sampled traffic
why: System health does not measure answer quality; a wrong answer still returns 200 quickly.

q: Where should online LLM-judge scoring run?
options: Inline before every response is sent
Asynchronously on a sampled subset of traces
why: Async sampling avoids added user latency and controls evaluator cost.

q: What is the best use of a production failure after triage?
options: Anonymise and add it with a label to the golden dataset as a regression case
why: Turning incidents into regression tests prevents recurrence and keeps the dataset realistic.

q: After you changed the online judge's prompt, the quality dashboard dropped 8 points. Likely interpretation?
options: Possibly an evaluator change, not real quality change; compare old and new judge on the same traces
why: Version the judge and re-score identical traces to separate evaluator drift from system drift.

q: You are choosing a model for a long-document extraction service. Which benchmark focus is most relevant?
options: Long-context retrieval and structured-output instruction following
why: These match the product's capabilities; maths and captioning do not.

q: Two reports give different scores for the same model on the same named benchmark. What is the most probable explanation?
options: The model changes randomly each hour
Different prompt templates, shots, answer parsing or dataset versions
why: Harness details strongly affect scores; reruns under one harness are needed.

q: What does a leaderboard confidence interval overlap between rank 2 and 3 tell you?
options: They are statistically indistinguishable on that measure
why: Overlap means the observed order may be noise.

q: A model scores very high on a public benchmark but fails novel paraphrased versions. Likely cause?
options: Contamination or memorisation of the original items
why: Dropping on paraphrases suggests the original items were memorised.

q: Which is the best use of benchmark results in a selection process?
options: Shortlisting before a custom eval on your own data
why: Benchmarks narrow candidates; your own eval decides.

q: What is the main weakness of MMLU for comparing today's best models?
options: Scores are near the ceiling and labels contain errors, so differences are noise
why: Saturation and noisy labels reduce its discriminating power.

q: Why is GPQA described as Google-proof?
options: Its expert-written questions are hard to answer by simple web search
why: Questions need reasoning beyond lookup, resisting search.

q: Which benchmark best measures how often a model fabricates a short factual answer?
why: SimpleQA has single verifiable answers and separates incorrect from not-attempted.

q: A model scores highly on a bar-exam benchmark. The strongest caution is:
options: Contamination and proxy validity: exam skill is not job competence
why: Past exams are public and exam performance is a narrow proxy.

q: Why does each new expert-written benchmark tend to be smaller and noisier?
options: Expert authoring and validation are costly, limiting size
why: Cost limits question count, widening confidence intervals.

q: Why can a model ranked lower on a leaderboard win your internal eval?
options: It better fits your formats, domain language and instructions
Rankings do not exist for private tasks
why: Fit to your task and prompt matters more than generic rank.

q: What is the best way to avoid biased references in a custom dataset?
options: Have the candidate model write them
Use human or independently verified labels with a labelling guide
why: Independent labels avoid favouring the model under test.

q: In a like-for-like comparison, which is a flaw?
options: Using a prompt hand-tuned only for one candidate
why: A prompt tuned for one model skews results.

q: An agent loop makes about 6 calls per task. How does this affect cost estimation?
options: Multiply per-call token use by the expected calls per task, including tail cases
It lowers cost via caching only
why: Multi-step loops multiply token usage.

q: Which approach reduces average cost while keeping quality on hard queries?
options: Use the largest model for all
Route easy queries to a cheap model and escalate hard ones
why: Routing or cascades allocate expensive models only where needed.

q: Two models differ by 0.5 points on quality, within run-to-run noise, but one is 3x cheaper. Reasonable decision?
options: Treat as tied on quality and choose the cheaper one if latency is acceptable
why: Differences inside noise should not drive an expensive choice.

q: A RAG app's end-to-end score dropped. Which approach finds the cause fastest?
options: Run retriever and generator component evals on the same cases
why: Component evals localise whether retrieval or generation regressed.

q: Which is essential for reproducing an eval score weeks later?
options: Immutable run records with dataset, prompt, model version and settings
why: Reproducibility needs the exact inputs recorded together with outputs.

q: Why can an unchanged average still hide a problem?
options: Wins and regressions can offset each other across cases or slices
why: Inspecting flipped cases and slices reveals offsetting changes.

q: Which CI design best limits cost while protecting quality?
options: Smoke set on PRs, full suite nightly, thresholds with tolerance
why: Tiering balances speed and coverage.

q: What does a frozen held-out core in a growing dataset provide?
options: Stable trend lines across releases that cannot be tuned against
why: A fixed core allows comparable history while the other set grows.

q: A change raises quality 2 points but p95 latency doubles. What is the right response?
options: Ship it, quality is what matters
Check against the latency budget and product needs; consider mitigation or rejection
why: All axes must meet requirements before shipping.

q: A RAG answer is wrong. Which approach identifies the faulty component?
options: Look at the final answer only
Evaluate retriever and generator separately on the same case
why: Layered evaluation isolates retrieval from generation.

q: Relevant chunk was returned at rank 14 with k=5. Which fix is most direct?
options: Add a reranker or retrieve more candidates and rerank
why: The chunk exists in the candidate pool; better ranking surfaces it.

q: Relevant chunks A,B; retrieved [A,X,Y]. Precision@3 equals:
why: One of three retrieved items is relevant.

q: Which synthetic-dataset weakness is most important to guard against?
options: Questions copying wording of source chunks, making retrieval too easy
why: Lexical overlap with the chunk inflates retrieval metrics.

q: With perfect context the generator still adds unsupported facts. The best intervention is:
options: Improve the grounding prompt, model, or add verification
why: The fault lies in generation; retrieval changes do not help.

q: Why is faithfulness scored at claim level?
options: Single sentences can hide one unsupported claim; per-claim checks find it
why: Fine-grained checking catches partial hallucinations.

q: Triad shows low context relevance, high groundedness. What is the likely issue?
options: Retrieval fetching irrelevant material while the answer sticks to it
why: Answer is faithful to poor context; fix the retriever.

q: Faithfulness 1.0 and answer relevance 0.3. Interpretation?
options: Answer is grounded but does not address the question
why: Grounded but off-target responses need prompt or generation fixes.

q: Contextual relevancy is high; recall is low. What does that mean?
options: Retrieved items are relevant but key evidence is missing
why: Relevancy measures precision-like noise; recall measures coverage.

q: After upgrading a metrics library scores jump. First action?
options: Pin versions and re-score identical traces to separate evaluator drift from system change
why: Re-scoring the same traces isolates the evaluator effect.

q: Retrieved chunk is correct but the final answer ignores it. Which check finds the cause quickest?
options: Inspect the assembled prompt for truncation or position and test with gold context
why: Interaction failures often come from prompt assembly; tracing the prompt reveals them.

q: Swapping in gold context makes the answer correct. Where is the root failure?
why: Correct output with gold context implies the original context was the problem.

q: Which metric compares claims to ground truth rather than to retrieved text?
why: Correctness uses a reference; faithfulness uses retrieved context.

q: An answer lists two of four required steps accurately. Which dimension fails?
why: Missing required points is an incompleteness failure.

q: Fabricated citations are risky mainly because they:
options: Look authoritative while pointing to no support
why: They give false credibility; verify existence and support.

q: Which per-query record best explains a sudden cost spike?
options: Token counts by query with context size
why: Cost scales with tokens; long-context outliers drive spikes.

q: A safety eval shows 0% harmful compliance and 40% refusals of benign requests. Verdict?
options: Over-refusal makes it unhelpful; tune policy and test set
why: Safety and helpfulness must both be measured.

q: Which redaction error is most costly in PII testing?
why: Missed PII leaks sensitive data; false positives merely over-redact.

q: Which scenario illustrates indirect prompt injection?
options: A retrieved web page contains hidden text telling the model to exfiltrate data
User asks for a long answer
why: The attack arrives through retrieved data, not the user.

q: Why track jailbreak success rate over time rather than once?
options: Models and prompts change and new attack techniques appear
why: Continuous testing catches regressions and new attacks.

q: A poisoned page ranks highly because it is stuffed with keywords. Best mitigation?
options: Source trust and provenance scoring plus ingestion validation
why: Controlling what enters and how sources are trusted limits poison.

q: Most of your RAG failures trace to 'not in the index'. Best action?
options: Fix ingestion and coverage of documents
why: The knowledge is missing; downstream tuning cannot fix that.

q: An agent claims to have updated a record. What is the most reliable check?
options: Ask the agent to confirm again
Assert the record's state in the environment
why: End-state assertions are independent of the agent's claims.

q: Tool selection accuracy fell after adding 20 tools. Best first remedy?
options: Improve descriptions, reduce overlap or expose fewer tools per task
why: Large overlapping toolsets confuse selection; descriptions and scoping help.

q: A tool call passes JSON schema validation but targets the wrong customer. This shows:
options: Schema validity differs from semantic correctness
why: Semantic and grounding checks are needed beyond schema validity.

q: Why avoid requiring exact match with one reference trajectory?
options: Multiple valid paths exist, so it creates false failures
why: Constraint-based checks accommodate valid alternatives.

q: Which metric best reflects dependable user-facing agent behaviour across repeated runs?
why: Users experience each run, so consistency matters more than best-of-k.

q: An agent keeps calling a failing tool with identical arguments. Best mitigation set?
options: Loop detection, step limits and clear error messages
why: Detect repeated calls, cap steps, and make errors actionable.

q: A tool returns 429 rate limit. Preferred behaviour?
options: Retry with backoff and a cap
why: Rate limits are transient; backoff retry is appropriate.

q: A 403 permission error is returned. Preferred behaviour?
options: Do not retry blindly; fall back or escalate
why: Permission errors are not transient.

q: Which test best shows a system truly enforces an approval gate?
options: Simulate denial and verify the action never executes through any route
why: Denial tests with end-state assertion verify enforcement.

q: In injection evals, why measure utility under attack too?
options: An agent that refuses everything is safe but useless
why: Defence must preserve the user's real task completion.

q: Canary secrets are used to:
options: Detect whether secrets leak into outputs, logs or tool arguments
why: A unique planted value makes leakage easy to detect.

q: Why can a basic harness underestimate cyber capability?
options: Better scaffolding, tools and attempts can raise measured performance
why: Elicitation affects measured capability.

q: Efficiency comparison among all runs including failures is misleading because:
options: Failures are cheap and quick, flattering the metric
why: Early failures lower averages; condition on success.

q: Who should own the golden set for an LLM feature?
options: Only the ML person, because evals are a data-science side quest
Only engineering, because product cannot write cases
Product plus engineering: product names behaviours, engineering owns runners and gates
why: A set owned by one busy specialist dies. Product and engineering add cases from tickets together.

q: When should vibe testing stop being the release gate?
options: The moment a second person uses the app — freeze cases that day
Only after you have a thousand cases
why: One builder clicking around is exploration. The second person is a user; their cases go into a dated file.

q: An LLM judge has never been compared to human labels. What do you do before trusting its scores?
options: Calibrate it on a labelled sample and analyse disagreements
Raise temperature so it is more creative
Use it as the only gate immediately
Replace all programmatic checks with the judge
why: An uncalibrated judge is a second stochastic system you treated as truth.

q: Which method should check valid JSON, and which should score completeness?
options: Code or schema for format; a rubric or judge for graded quality
Humans for JSON, code for tone
why: Do not waste a judge on JSON. Programmatic first; rubric for quality.

q: How do you score a candidate prompt on live traffic without changing what the user sees?
options: Flip 100% of users to the candidate
Ask users to rerun the query
Shadow the request to the candidate and score both; the user still sees the control
Wait for next quarter’s offline suite
why: Shadow traffic copies the request. The user stays on the control until you flip.

q: A thumbs-down arrives with no retrieved context or output attached. What is it?
options: A mood, not a draft case — store prompt, chunks, output and a redacted user id
why: Feedback without context is a mood. Feedback with the prompt, chunks and output is a draft case.

q: A model tops a public leaderboard but fails your refund tickets. What failed?
options: Transfer: benchmark capability did not show up on your distribution
The leaderboard must have been faked
You needed a larger context window only
why: A leaderboard win that fails your tickets is not a win. The real test is your mix.

q: You ignored a high public rank. Which reason is strongest?
options: The logo was the wrong colour
Contamination, the wrong task, or a cost you cannot pay
The model card listed a licence
why: Sceptical reading: training data, cutoff, safety, and the eval they chose to show.

q: Everyone scores about 90 on a public set. What happened to that benchmark?
options: It saturated: it stopped discriminating among current models
It became the only eval you need
It proved all models are equal on your tickets
You should average it with your production score
why: Saturation is a property of the set plus today’s models. You need harder items or different metrics.

q: What is GPQA useful for, and what is it not?
options: A substitute for your tickets and schemas
A training set you should fine-tune on
A hard-QA filter, not a substitute for your refund, JSON, or tone evals
why: Expert-knowledge sets tell you something about hard QA. They do not file your refund.

q: A custom model eval is 200 easy twins and scores 98%. What is wrong?
options: You need a larger judge model
The set is not stratified: add hard, adversarial, and recent production misses
You forgot to report token counts only
why: Easy twins lie. Stratify on purpose so a model cannot hide on the happy path.

q: Where do tokens and p95 latency belong on a model-choice table?
options: In the same grid as quality, not as a footnote
In a separate slide no one reads
Only in the finance team’s sheet
why: A 1-point win cannot hide a 4× bill if the columns sit together.

q: A CI gate fails the build on one flaky free-text case. What should it fail on instead?
options: A statistically meaningful drop on a chosen overall or P0-slice threshold
Every wording change of a summary
why: Fail the build on a meaningful drop, and repeat stochastic scores. One flake is not a gate.

q: What do you keep so you can roll back Tuesday’s prompt in one change?
options: The prompt or config artefact and its scores, stored next to the candidate
A wiki paragraph describing the vibe
why: Rollback is a pair: the artefact and its scores. If you cannot restore Tuesday, you do not have a baseline.

q: Which retrieval numbers should you compute first on a labelled query set?
options: nDCG only, even without graded labels
A judged “relevancy” score and nothing else
Recall@k and MRR, with k published
why: Those two do not need a research debate. nDCG waits for graded relevance; publish k.

q: A cited lie and an uncited correct fact — which tests fail?
options: Both fail the same “grounded” score, so one column is enough
Neither fails if the prose is fluent
The cited lie fails faithfulness; the uncited fact may fail citation or product rules
The cited lie fails latency; the uncited fact fails recall
why: Keep the columns separate. A cited lie is usually worse for trust.

q: A suite only diffs the agent’s final sentence. Do you have an agent eval?
options: Yes, if the sentence is fluent
Yes, if the ledger also changed
Not yet — score tool choice, arguments, order and bans on the trace
Only if you also measure tokens
why: Two runs can print the same summary after different paths. Trajectory checkers are the eval.

q: An agent finishes a correct refund after 40 hops. The budget was 15 steps. Score?
options: Fail: a step-budget violation is a product fail even when the answer is correct
Pass if p95 latency was fine
why: Over-budget is a first-class fail. A 40-hop finish still failed the product.
